newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesia high short-term rates seen temporary.
newsitem.headline: Indonesia high short-term rates seen temporary.

text.p: Indonesia's high short-term interest rate policy is likely to be temporary and not have a full-scale impact on the economy, bank treasurers said on Wednesday.
They said the central bank had been keeping short-term interest rates artificially high to ward off speculative dollar buying in the aftermath of the region's recent currency crises.
The central bank, Bank Indonesia, raised its benchmark overnight rates of central bank certificates (SBIs) to 14.0 percent on July 24 and has since kept the rates at that level.
SBI overnight rates were usually around five to six percent before the region's currency woes hit Indonesia.
SBIs are short-term rupiah-denominated obligations issued by the central bank to drain liquidity from the market.
Treasurers said the central bank was likely to maintain its tight grip on short-term money until regional markets stabilised.
"I don't think the high short-term rates policy will last for long. It's only temporary," Saleh Aziz, treasury manager at the PT Bank Export Import Indonesia, told Reuters.
Aziz said the general perception was also reflected by inverse interest rates in the interbank market where short-term rates were higher than longer-term ones.
Overnight rupiah was traded at 21.0 percent, compared with three-month money at 18.5 percent on Wednesday.
"Offshore fund managers, with some 'good names' are looking for rupiah assets currently to lock in attractive rates because they think it won't last for long," Aziz said.

Pardy Kendy, treasury head of PT Bank Buana Indonesia, shared the same view, adding that if the central bank wanted to maintain a high interest rate environment, the bank would have raised its benchmark rates for all maturities.
"But what we see, the central bank only raises rates of very short-term paper while keeping others stable," he said.

One-week SBI rates were 10.0 percent on Wednesday, compared with 6.5 percent in early July. But the longer the terms were, the smaller the increase. Three-month SBIs were 11.0 percent against 10.75 percent in July while the one-year rate was stable.
Kendy said the central bank's attempt to keep short-term rates expensive was aimed at reducing speculative dollar buying using cheap rupiah financing.
He said a full-scale impact on the economy was unlikely if the policy was kept temporary, but banks relying on money market funds would be affected with increased borrowing costs.
"But I think banks with a strong deposit-base will keep a wait-and-see attitude unless this condition lasts for more than a month," Kendy said.
Treasurers said the rupiah appeared to stabilise around the 2,600 a dollar zone which was within the area the central bank felt comfortable with under current condition.
The central bank said after the rupiah reached a low of 2,663 against the dollar on July 21 that the currency had in recent days returned to a normal level of between 2,555 and 2,610 rupiah.
The assault on the rupiah followed speculative attacks on other regional currencies, with market-forced devaluations in the Thai baht and the Philippine peso.

Economists said the range mentioned by the central bank would also help Indonesia remain competitive with its neighbours after factoring in a plunge of 25 percent in Thailand's baht and some 10 percent in the peso.

The rupiah, which started the year at 2,363 per dollar, had depreciated almost 10 percent by Wednesday, compared with the government's unofficial annual depreciation target of about four to five percent.
The rupiah depreciated less than four percent last year.
